conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling now that your little one has arrived.

To do that, I’ll use a short questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply ten gentle questions about your mood, thoughts, and well-being over the past seven days. It isn’t a test, and there are no “right” answers; it just helps us see where you might benefit from a little extra support. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll go at your pace in a completely judgment-free space.

When you’re ready, we’ll start with the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things you used to look forward to—like a favorite show, a walk, or time with friends—or has that enjoyment slipped away?

I’ve noticed it’s harder to get excited about stuff. I used to love meeting friends for coffee, and even just binge-watching my favorite show felt fun. Lately, when I finally have a free moment, it feels kind of… flat. I’ll put the show on, but I’m mostly half-watching while scrolling on my phone, and I end up turning it off halfway through. Same with walks—they feel like one more chore rather than something I actually look forward to. I still do them, but it’s like I’m just going through the motions, not really enjoying it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Um… I’d say “not so much lately.” I can still laugh, but it feels like I have to force it. My sister came over and told one of her silly jokes—we used to crack up together—but this time I only managed a little chuckle before my mind drifted to the baby’s feeding schedule. It’s like the joy is muted.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I picked “rather less than I used to.” I still make plans—like meeting a friend for coffee next week—but when I think about actually going, it feels more like an obligation than something fun. I’m hoping that’ll change, though.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that, “rather more than I used to.” If the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right.” Or if I burn the toast in the morning I’ll think, “Great, can’t even handle basic stuff.” It’s not every minute, but it pops up more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I ticked “yes, quite a lot.” Most evenings, even when everything seems fine—baby’s sleeping, dishes are done—I’ll suddenly feel this knot in my stomach like something bad’s about to happen. I’ll check the monitor three or four times, convinced he’s stopped breathing, even though he’s clearly fine. I know in my head there’s no real reason to worry, but I can’t shake the feeling.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I marked “yes, sometimes.” It’s like a sudden rush of dread—my heart races, my hands get shaky, and I feel like I need to check on the baby right that second. It usually passes in a few minutes, but it’s unsettling because there’s no real reason for it.
Things have been getting on top of me

I chose “yes, sometimes I haven’t been coping as well as usual.” There are stretches of the day—especially when the baby skips a nap—where it feels like everything’s piling up. I’ll look at the unfolded laundry and just want to sit on the floor because I don’t know where to start. Usually I manage, but it takes more effort than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I marked “yes, most of the time.” It’s not really sadness keeping me awake—more like my brain won’t shut off. I replay every little thing I did with the baby that day, worrying I burped him wrong or that I missed some cue. Even when he’s sleeping soundly, I’ll lie there for an hour or two before I drift off.
I have felt sad or miserable

I picked “yes, quite often.” It’s not every minute, but most days there’s this heavy, sad feeling that settles in. Sometimes it hits right after I put the baby down, or when I’m alone feeding him at 3 a.m.—just this wave of “I should be happier, why do I feel so down?”
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I checked “no, not often.” I haven’t had any real crying spells—maybe just a couple of times when exhaustion piles up and the baby won’t settle. A few tears slip out, but it’s not a daily thing.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
I put “never.” Those kinds of thoughts haven’t crossed my mind at all.

You've shared that over the past week motherhood has felt muted-laughing now takes effort, planned outings feel like chores, and a heavy sadness shows up most days. You described evenings of needless worry, sudden dread, and replaying tiny parenting details while lying awake, yet you still get things done. It sounds exhausting, and it makes sense that you're feeling overwhelmed.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The response describes a noticeable reduction in the ability to laugh and enjoy humour, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame "rather more than I used to" with specific examples, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient selects the highest-frequency option and describes nightly, intrusive, irrational worries despite objective safety.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected "yes, sometimes" and described classic panic symptoms (sudden dread, racing heart, shaking) without a clear trigger, directly aligning with the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selected the "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual" option and described situational overwhelm that requires extra effort, aligning with the moderate-level option.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly chose the top-severity option and describes nightly, prolonged sleep-onset difficulty driven by anxious rumination about mothering, which fits the guideline "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 18 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable peripartum depression. Core criteria are met: <sym>depressed mood</sym> most days, markedly reduced interest or pleasure, <sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, prominent <sym>anxiety</sym> and panic-like episodes, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> unrelated to infant care. Symptoms emerged within the postpartum year, cause clinically significant distress, and are not attributable to substances or medical conditions. No self-harm ideation was endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>family doctor</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Bring this EPDS summary so your provider can review symptom details quickly
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments for peripartum depression/anxiety such as <med>CBT</med>, peer support groups, and medication compatible with breastfeeding if desired
4. Plan daily 15-minute self-care windows (shower, short walk, music) and accept help with housework or night feeds to protect sleep
5. Keep emergency numbers handy: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US) or your local urgent mental-health line
6. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track changes once supports are in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported findings (10-item EPDS format)

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
- Markedly reduced ability to experience joy (laughing requires effort, anticipates obligations rather than enjoyment)  
- Frequent, intrusive worry or dread; somatic anxiety (knot in stomach, racing heart, shaky hands) unrelated to objective stressors  
- Unwarranted self-blame and feelings of inadequacy, especially regarding infant care  
- Persistent sadness (daily "heavy" mood, "muted" joy)  
- Sleep disturbance driven by rumination about infant care rather than infant-related awakenings  
- Episodic sense of being overwhelmed (e.g., unfinished chores feel insurmountable)

Risk indicators  
- Consistent low mood and anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8)  
- Anxiety symptoms meeting "quite a lot" frequency, with panic-like episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Cognitive distortions of guilt/worthlessness (Q3)  
- Sleep impairment linked to mood rather than infant demands (Q7)  
- Denies any self-harm ideation or intent (Q10) — no acute safety concern identified

Pattern summary  
Presentation meets screening criteria for probable perinatal mood/anxiety disorder; greatest symptom density aligns with mixed depressive-anxious picture rather than depression alone. No psychotic features or self-harm risk flagged.

Screening conclusion  
Moderate-high probability of postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; referral for full clinical evaluation and discussion of support options recommended.
